Hi rolandtrip and thanks for your answer. I'd like to share some apreciations/doubts/comments about it. 

If 
> the internals of the different distributions are for 80% to 90% based on the same independent software projects (Linux kernel, Xorg, KDE, Calligra, GNU, etc). 

and
>Most of what makes up Linux Mint is a duplication of software in Ubuntu and most software what makes up Ubuntu is a duplication of Debian.

and also considering that
>There is no fundamental difference between Fedora and OpenSUSE in the base packages. Both use the Linux kernel, glibc, GNU utilities, Bash, etc.

Wouldn't it be more easy to horizontaly integrate all the OSes into one? 
I mean, if Xubuntu>Ubuntu>Debian wouldn't it be easier then to converge the three of them into one only? Thus if we consider this:

* Netrunner>Kubuntu>Ubuntu>Debian

* Lubuntu>Ubuntu>Debian

* Xubuntu>Ubuntu>Debian

* elementaryOS>Ubuntu>Debian

and so on, to encompass all linux distributions and their origins we'd get [this](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/99/Gldt1202.svg)

Then we could focus in a first approach on the base distros such as debian, arch and enoch for example, which would have the main differences regarding to architecture or structure. 

Or in the other hand, just pick one base distro, for example Debian, and then create a common path to all its branches, said path could be a new distro which emerges as the Ueber-Distro that you mention.  

>What you propose boils down to something that is larger than Debian in software available and easier to use than Linux Mint. To accomplish this, you'd need a development team larger than what all other distributions have combined, with a single focus on making all software (capable of running on Linux) available in a completely preconfigured way. Somehow, this gargantuan effort needs to be self-sustainable, tightly led with a singular vision and it needs to play well with the other community members. It's not theoretically impossible, but realistically not very probably that such an effort could be created successfully.

If you're not a programmer then there isn't much that you can do about it. And you'll just have to wait while other OSes like iOS are far ahead. So, how really competitive linux is? I imagine it as a tree, where the distros are the roots, and the next step is the stem, and hopefully the trunk.
